# Section A: everyone (questions 1 to 43)

These questions are about Git and GitHub, GitHub Actions, Quarto [@quarto], ggplot2 [@ggplot2], tinytable [@tinytable], working with data, and the Donaldson paper in @Alexander2023.

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**1.** Which statement is correct?

(A) GitHub is the software on your laptop; Git is the website where the repositories are hosted
(B) Git only works while you are connected to GitHub, because the history is stored on the website
(C) Git and GitHub are two names for the same thing; the software was renamed when Microsoft bought it
(D) Git is version control software on your laptop; GitHub is a website that hosts Git repositories

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**2.** You changed `paper.qmd` and `notes.txt`, but only want the changes to `paper.qmd` in the next snapshot. What do you run first?

(A) `git add paper.qmd`
(B) `git push`
(C) `git add .`
(D) `git commit -m "Update paper"`

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**3.** In which order do you run these to get your local changes onto GitHub?

(A) commit, add, push
(B) add, push, commit
(C) add, commit, push
(D) push, add, commit

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**4.** Which commit message will be most useful to you in three weeks?

(A) "Fixed the problem from yesterday"
(B) "Made some more changes to paper.qmd"
(C) "Update graph, fix typos, add data, rewrite intro, change references"
(D) "Add histogram of occupancy rate to data section"

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**5.** What does the Donaldson paper rubric ask for with respect to commits?

(A) One commit when the paper is finished, so that the history is clean
(B) Commit messages that begin with the date
(C) A commit every time a file is saved
(D) At least a handful of commits, with meaningful messages

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**6.** `git push` fails because "the remote contains work that you do not have locally". What should you do next?

(A) `git pull`, deal with any conflicts, then push again
(B) `git push --force`, so that your version wins
(C) Make a new branch and push that instead, leaving `main` as it is
(D) Delete your local copy, clone again, and redo your changes by hand

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**7.** After a pull you find `<<<<<<< HEAD`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` inside `paper.qmd`. What has happened, and what do you do?

(A) Two edits to the same lines could not be merged; keep what you want, delete the markers, then add and commit
(B) The pull is only half finished; run `git pull` again and the markers will be removed for you
(C) Git has already kept the newer of the two versions; delete the markers and commit the file as it is
(D) The file was damaged during the pull; discard it with `git checkout paper.qmd`, and then pull again

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**8.** What is a pull request for?

(A) To download the latest version of a repository; it is GitHub's name for `git pull`
(B) To make a private backup of your branch on GitHub, which only you are able to see
(C) To report a problem or ask a question about a repository, so the owner can respond
(D) To propose changes from a branch or fork, so they can be reviewed before they are merged

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**9.** You want to add your group's slides to the class repo, which you do not own. What is the usual route?

(A) Open an issue on the class repo and attach the slides
(B) Clone the class repo, add the slides, and push to `main`
(C) Download the repo as a zip, add the slides, and upload it as a new repo of your own
(D) Fork the repo, make the change in your fork, then open a pull request

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**10.** Which of these belongs in `.gitignore`?

(A) `references.bib`
(B) `.env`, containing your API key
(C) `data/analysis_data.parquet`, which the paper reads
(D) `README.md`

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**11.** Where does a GitHub Actions workflow run?

(A) On your laptop, whenever you push
(B) On a fresh computer that GitHub provides, when a trigger you specified happens
(C) On your laptop, but only if it is switched on at the scheduled time
(D) On a computer that GitHub provides, using the Python and packages installed on your laptop

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**12.** A workflow has `cron: '0 7 * * *'`. When does it run?

(A) Every 7 minutes
(B) On the 7th day of each month
(C) Every day at 7:00 Toronto time
(D) Every day at 7:00 UTC

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**13.** The Bluesky example needs a password. Where should the password live?

(A) In the script itself, since the repo is private and only collaborators can read the code
(B) In a `.env` file that is committed to the repo, so that the workflow is able to load it
(C) As a repository secret in GitHub's settings, passed to the script as an environment variable

# Section B: everyone, statistical learning (questions 44 to 53)

These questions are about the ideas in Chapter 2.1 of @James2023, "What is Statistical Learning?".

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**44.** In the model $Y = f(X) + \epsilon$, what is $\epsilon$?

(A) A random error term, independent of $X$, with mean zero
(B) The gap between the training data and the test data
(C) Measurement error in $X$, which biases the estimate of $f$
(D) The part of $f$ that the chosen method is unable to capture

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**45.** What is the difference between reducible and irreducible error?

(A) Reducible error falls as more predictors are measured; irreducible error comes from choosing a model that is too simple
(B) Reducible error is the error made on the training data; irreducible error is the error made on observations not yet seen
(C) Reducible error comes from estimating $f$ imperfectly; irreducible error comes from $\epsilon$, and remains even if $f$ is known
(D) Reducible error comes from $\epsilon$; irreducible error comes from estimating $f$ imperfectly, and remains whatever method is used

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**46.** Which of these is a question of inference rather than prediction?

(A) Which characteristics of a shelter are associated with higher occupancy?
(B) Which of the city's shelter programs will be over capacity tomorrow night?
(C) How many people will be staying in Toronto's shelters next Tuesday night?
(D) What occupancy rate should be expected at a new shelter that has 60 beds?

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**47.** When the goal is prediction, how is the estimate $\hat{f}$ usually treated?

(A) As known in advance, so that it does not depend on the training data
(B) As linear, because only a linear model gives predictions that are valid
(C) As a black box: its exact form matters little if its predictions are accurate
(D) As the object of interest: each part of it must have a clear interpretation

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**48.** What are the two steps of a parametric approach to estimating $f$?

(A) Split the data into training and test sets, then average the estimates from each
(B) Rank the predictors by their correlation with $Y$, then keep the strongest of them
(C) Assume a functional form for $f$, then use the training data to estimate its parameters
(D) Estimate $f$ with no assumed form, then summarise that estimate with a few parameters

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**49.** What is the main disadvantage of a parametric approach?

(A) A very large number of observations is needed before $f$ is estimated accurately
(B) The assumed form may be far from the true $f$, in which case the estimate is poor
(C) It can be used only when the response is quantitative, and not when it is a category
(D) The fitted model has no coefficients, so there is nothing that can be interpreted

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**50.** What is the trade-off with non-parametric methods?

(A) They can fit many shapes of $f$, but need far more observations to do so accurately
(B) They need far fewer observations, but can fit only shapes of $f$ that are nearly linear
(C) They give results that are easier to interpret, but their predictions are less accurate
(D) They cannot overfit, because they make no assumption at all about the form of $f$

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**51.** Why might you choose a restrictive method, such as linear regression, over a more flexible one?

(A) A flexible method cannot be fitted when there are more than a few predictors
(B) A restrictive method has lower bias, so its estimates are nearer the truth
(C) A restrictive method always predicts better on new data than a flexible one
(D) When inference is the goal, a restrictive model is much easier to interpret

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**52.** What distinguishes supervised from unsupervised learning?

(A) In supervised learning the predictors are numeric; in unsupervised learning they are categories
(B) In supervised learning the method is parametric; in unsupervised learning it is non-parametric
(C) In supervised learning every observation has a response; in unsupervised learning there is none
(D) In supervised learning a person checks each prediction; in unsupervised learning nobody checks

\needspace{7\baselineskip}
**53.** Which of these is a classification problem rather than a regression problem?

(A) Predicting which candidate a survey respondent will vote for
(B) Predicting the share of the vote that a candidate will receive
(C) Predicting how many people will be in shelters tomorrow night
(D) Predicting a respondent's feeling-thermometer score out of 100
